0.title: Knowing the God Who Is
0.essay:
Everyone has a picture of God. Some picture a stern judge, some a distant force, some an indulgent friend who never minds what we do. Most of us carry a mixture, shaped more by our upbringing and moods than by the Bible. And the picture matters, because we become like what we worship, and we trust only as far as we know.

God’s self-introduction

The attributes of God are the truths Scripture tells us about what God is like: that he is eternal, unchanging, present everywhere, all-knowing, all-powerful, wise, just, good, loving, merciful, patient and faithful. They are not a list of abstract properties for theologians. They are God’s own self-introduction. When Moses asked to see God’s glory, God answered by proclaiming his name and his character (Exodus 34:6–7). To know God’s attributes is to know God as he has chosen to be known.

Why it is so practical

Almost every struggle of the Christian life is, at bottom, a question about what God is like. A Christian facing a frightening diagnosis needs to know that God is all-powerful and all-wise. A believer who has failed badly needs to know that God is merciful and patient. Someone who has been wronged needs to know that God is just. A grieving widow needs to know that God is faithful and does not change.

The chapters

We begin with how God makes himself known. Then we consider God in himself: eternal, independent and unchanging. Next, God everywhere, all-knowing and all-powerful. Then God righteous and wrathful; then God of love, goodness, mercy and patience; and finally God faithful and true.

Three of God’s attributes have studies of their own: the Holiness of God, the Grace of God and the Sovereignty of God. This study gathers the rest and shows how they all belong together in the one living God.

1.title: How God Makes Himself Known
1.essay:
We cannot discover God by our own cleverness. He is infinite and we are finite; he is the Creator and we are creatures. If we are to know him at all, he must make himself known. And he has.

Creation, Scripture and Christ

“The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 19:1). God’s “invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made” (Romans 1:20). But creation tells us only so much. In Scripture God speaks, and in Jesus Christ he comes in person: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). Every attribute of God is seen most clearly in the face of Christ.

The name God proclaimed

The richest Old Testament description of God came at a dark moment. Israel had just worshipped the golden calf. Moses pleaded with God not to abandon his people and asked, “Please show me your glory” (Exodus 33:18). God hid him in a cleft of the rock and passed by, proclaiming his name: “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty” (Exodus 34:6–7).

God’s glory, it turns out, is above all his character. And notice what he emphasises. Mercy, grace, patience, steadfast love and faithfulness come first and take up most of the description. Justice is there too: he will not clear the guilty. Both are real; neither cancels the other. But God wants to be known first as the God who abounds in steadfast love. This self-description echoes through the Psalms, the prophets and even Jonah’s complaint.

How can a God who forgives iniquity also refuse to clear the guilty? The Old Testament leaves the tension standing. The cross resolves it: there God forgave sinners because he punished their sin in his Son, so that he is “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).

The point of our lives

Knowing God is not a detour from the Christian life; it is the heart of it. “Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me” (Jeremiah 9:23–24). And God says what he delights in: steadfast love, justice and righteousness. His attributes are not grudging duties but what he loves to do.

Jesus defines eternal life itself in these terms: “this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). Eternal life is a relationship before it is a length of time.

How the attributes fit together

Some attributes belong to God alone: that he depends on nothing, never changes, is eternal and is present everywhere. We will never share these, and they teach us humility and worship. Others God shares, in creaturely measure, with those made in his image: wisdom, goodness, love, mercy, justice, holiness and faithfulness. These show us what he is making us into (Ephesians 5:1).

And God is not made of parts, as if he were partly loving and partly just. Every attribute describes the whole God. His love is a just love, and his justice a loving justice; his power is always wise, and his wisdom always powerful. So we must never set one attribute against another, as though God’s love had to overcome his holiness.

We know God truly, because he has spoken truly. But we will never know him exhaustively, even in eternity. After eleven chapters explaining God’s plan of salvation, Paul does not summarise; he sings: “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Romans 11:33). Good theology always ends in praise.

Right doctrine, right heart

Jonah knew God’s attributes well, and they made him angry. When God spared Nineveh, he complained, “I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love” (Jonah 4:2) — quoting Exodus 34. He had the right doctrine and the wrong heart. Knowing God is meant to make us love what God loves, even his mercy to our enemies.

A young Christian realised her picture of God came mostly from her father, who was hard to please and quick to criticise. She had always assumed God was disappointed in her. As she read Exodus 34 and Psalm 103 slowly, she saw she had been worshipping a God who does not exist. The real God is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love. Her obedience did not stop — but it began to come from gratitude rather than fear.

For reflection

Finish the sentence, “God is the kind of God who…” Does your answer come from Scripture or from experience? Read Exodus 34:6–7 aloud: which phrase do you most need to believe this week? How does Jesus show you what God is like? Choose one scene from the Gospels.

2.title: God in Himself: Eternal, Independent, Unchanging
2.essay:
When Moses asked for God’s name at the burning bush, God answered, “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14). Everything else in the universe is what it is because something else made it so. God simply is. He is not becoming, not growing, not depending on anything outside himself. He is the one fixed point of reality.

The God who needs nothing

God is independent. Paul told the philosophers of Athens, in a city full of temples and offerings, that God is not “served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything” (Acts 17:25). God did not create the world because he was lonely or incomplete. The Father, the Son and the Spirit lived in perfect love before anything was made (John 17:24). He created out of overflowing goodness, not need.

This is humbling, and it is freeing. We cannot add to God, and we cannot diminish him. Our worship does not supply something he lacks; it brings us into the joy he already has. And a God who needs nothing can never be manipulated, bribed or exhausted. He gives because he is generous, not because he owes us.

Yet the self-existent God immediately ties himself to people: he is “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:15). And Jesus took the divine name on his own lips: “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58).

The eternal God

“Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever you had formed the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting you are God” (Psalm 90:2). God has no beginning and no end. He is not trapped in time as we are, waiting for the future to arrive; he made time and rules over it. “With the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day” (2 Peter 3:8).

Psalm 90 is “A Prayer of Moses, the man of God”. Moses had buried a whole generation in the wilderness and knew how short life is: “The years of our life are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty” (Psalm 90:10). His comfort was not that life would last longer, but that God lasts for ever: “Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations” (Psalm 90:1). So he asks the eternal God to “establish the work of our hands” (Psalm 90:17), that brief lives might have lasting meaning.

The God who does not change

“For I the LORD do not change; therefore you, O children of Jacob, are not consumed” (Malachi 3:6). Malachi’s hearers had grown careless and cynical and deserved to be consumed. The only reason they had not been is that God does not change; he had made promises to Jacob, and he would keep them. If God’s love depended on our steadiness, we would be lost. It depends on his.

God does not grow wiser, kinder or stronger, because he is already infinitely all three. He does not grow weaker, more forgetful or less patient. James calls him “the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change” (James 1:17). The sun moves and shadows shift; God does not. Balaam, hired to curse Israel, found he could only bless them, and explained why: “God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind. Has he said, and will he not do it?” (Numbers 23:19). Every promise of God rests on that verse.

This does not make God cold or static. He acts, speaks, rescues and judges. He responds to prayer. But he always acts as the same God, according to the same character and the same eternal plan.

“God relented”

Several passages say God relented or regretted (Genesis 6:6; Exodus 32:14; Jonah 3:10). Yet in the very chapter where God says he regrets making Saul king, Samuel says God “is not a man, that he should have regret” (1 Samuel 15:29). Some conclude that God genuinely changes his mind because he does not know or has not settled the future. The better view fits all the texts: God never changes in character or purpose, and “relenting” describes a real change in how he deals with people when they change — a change he himself announced. “If that nation, concerning which I have spoken, turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it” (Jeremiah 18:8). When Nineveh repented, God did exactly what his unchanging character had always promised. The language is real, but spoken from our side of the story. It never means God was surprised, mistaken or fickle.

Does God feel? The historic confessions describe God as “without body, parts, or passions”. That does not make him unfeeling. He does not undergo moods forced on him from outside, but his love, joy, compassion and anger are real and perfect, the settled responses of his unchanging character. And the Son, having taken our human nature, truly wept and suffered.

Steady ground

A man in his seventies has seen almost everything change: his body, his career, his church, his country, his friendships. Many of those he loved are gone. One evening he reads Malachi 3:6 and Hebrews 13:8, “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” For the first time in years he feels steady ground under his feet. Everything else has moved. God has not.

For reflection

How does it change your prayers to know that God needs nothing from you? When circumstances change suddenly, do you assume God has changed toward you? How would you explain Jonah 3:10 to someone who thinks it proves God changes his mind?

3.title: Everywhere, All-Knowing, All-Powerful
3.essay:
Psalm 139 is the Bible’s great meditation on three attributes that belong to God alone: his knowledge, his presence and his power. And remarkably, David does not treat them as abstract ideas. He prays them.

The God who knows

“O LORD, you have searched me and known me! You know when I sit down and when I rise up; you discern my thoughts from afar” (Psalm 139:1–2). God knows our actions, our words before we speak them and our thoughts before we think them. He knows the number of the stars (Psalm 147:4) and the hairs on our heads (Matthew 10:30). He knows the future as surely as the past, “declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done” (Isaiah 46:10). Nothing has ever occurred to God. Nothing has ever surprised him. David’s response is to be overwhelmed: “Such knowledge is too wonderful for me” (Psalm 139:6).

Some modern teachers, called open theists, argue that God cannot know free choices not yet made, so that he takes risks, learns as history unfolds and is sometimes disappointed. Scripture is clear and repeated against this. God predicts free human actions centuries ahead — Cyrus by name (Isaiah 45:1) — and Peter’s denial that very night (Matthew 26:34). He knew all our days “when as yet there was none of them” (Psalm 139:16). In Isaiah, the ability to declare the future is the very proof that the LORD is God and the idols are not (Isaiah 41:22–23). A God who did not know the future could promise nothing with certainty.

Knowing everything is not the same as being wise. Wisdom is choosing the best ends by the best means. God is “the only wise God” (Romans 16:27), and his wisdom is seen above all in the cross, which looks like foolishness to the world (1 Corinthians 1:24–25).

The God who is everywhere

“Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence?” (Psalm 139:7). David imagines the heights, the grave, the far side of the sea, the darkness — and finds God already there, “for darkness is as light with you” (Psalm 139:12). This does not mean God is spread thinly through the universe like a gas, or that everything is God. It means the whole God is present to every part of his creation. “Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD” (Jeremiah 23:24). False prophets in Jeremiah’s day spoke lies in God’s name as if he could not hear. He hears. There is no place where God is absent — and so no place where his people are alone.

Hagar ran away from harsh treatment into the desert, alone and pregnant. There the angel of the LORD found her, and she named God: “You are a God of seeing” (Genesis 16:13). A runaway slave in the wilderness discovered she was not invisible.

The God who can do all he wills

Jerusalem was under siege when God told Jeremiah to buy a field — an absurd deal with the Babylonians at the gates. Jeremiah obeyed, then prayed: “Ah, Lord GOD! It is you who have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm! Nothing is too hard for you” (Jeremiah 32:17). Faith often means acting on God’s power before we can see how he will use it.

God’s power is never force without direction; it is always the power of his wisdom and goodness. There are things God cannot do: he cannot lie (Hebrews 6:18), cannot deny himself (2 Timothy 2:13) and cannot be tempted with evil (James 1:13). These are not limits on his power. They are the perfections of his character.

Babylon’s idols had to be carried on the backs of animals (Isaiah 46:1). The LORD is the opposite: he carries his people (Isaiah 46:4). History is not a series of accidents God tries to manage. It is the unfolding of his purpose.

Terror, or comfort?

For the unrepentant, these truths are terrifying: “no creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account” (Hebrews 4:13). For believers they are the deepest comfort. The God who knows everything about us has loved us anyway. The God who is everywhere is with us in the hospital room and the lonely flat. The God who can do anything is on our side.

A teenager struggling with a secret sin read Psalm 139 and felt exposed. God knew all of it. A wise pastor helped him read to the end, where David asks God to search him and “lead me in the way everlasting” (Psalm 139:24). The God who sees everything was not waiting to shame him, but ready to lead him out. The gospel turns the instinct to hide into the freedom to come near.

For reflection

Read Psalm 139:1–18. Which verse comforts you most, and which unsettles you? Where do you need to remember this week that God is with you? Why are the things God cannot do signs of perfection rather than weakness?

4.title: Righteous and Wrathful
4.essay:
Many people today are happy to believe in a loving God but recoil from a God of justice and wrath. Yet the Bible’s God is both — and if he were not just, he would not be good.

The Judge of all the earth

“The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice. A God of faithfulness and without iniquity, just and upright is he” (Deuteronomy 32:4). God always does what is right. He never takes bribes, never shows favouritism, never punishes the innocent or acquits the guilty. When Abraham pleaded for Sodom, bargaining from fifty righteous people down to ten, his boldness rested on one conviction: “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25). He was not trying to make God more just than he is, but appealing to the justice God already has. Every prayer for justice in a broken world stands on that question.

Holy opposition to evil

God’s wrath is his settled, holy opposition to evil. It is not a temper tantrum or wounded pride. It is what love and justice look like when they meet cruelty, lies and rebellion. A God who looked at child abuse, genocide and human trafficking and felt nothing would not be loving. “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth” (Romans 1:18). It is present now, as God hands people over to the sins they choose (Romans 1:24), and it will be revealed fully on the last day (Romans 2:5).

Paul’s explanation of the gospel begins with wrath, not because wrath matters more than love, but because the good news makes no sense until we see the bad news. And wrath is not the opposite of love; the opposite of love is indifference. Both God’s love and his anger flow from his holiness. He is angry at sin because he loves what sin destroys. Yet his wrath is never described as his delight. He is “slow to anger” but “abounding in steadfast love” (Exodus 34:6).

God is also jealous: “the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God” (Exodus 34:14). Human jealousy is often petty, but there is a right jealousy — a husband’s jealousy for his wife’s faithfulness. God will not share his people’s love with idols, because idols destroy those who worship them.

Patience is not endless

Nahum holds together what we tend to separate: “The LORD is a jealous and avenging God… The LORD is slow to anger and great in power, and the LORD will by no means clear the guilty” (Nahum 1:2–3). Nineveh had been spared in Jonah’s day, more than a century before. God’s patience is real, but it is not endless. For the Assyrians, whose empire had terrorised the nations, this was terrible news. For the peoples they had crushed it was comfort: “The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble” (Nahum 1:7). The same justice that terrifies the oppressor shelters the oppressed.

Where justice and mercy meet

Here is the answer to the riddle of Exodus 34:7. If God simply overlooked sin, he would cease to be just. If he punished every sinner, no one would be saved. At the cross he did both. God put forward Christ “as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith… so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:25–26). A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away wrath by bearing it. God did not lower his standard to save us; he met it himself. Jesus drank the cup of wrath so that those who trust in him never will. “Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God” (Romans 5:9).

Hell

Some evangelicals hold that the unrepentant will finally be destroyed and cease to exist. The historic view is that they will suffer conscious punishment for ever. Jesus sets the two destinies side by side with the same word: “these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46). If the life is endless, so is the punishment. Jesus spoke of hell more than anyone in Scripture — and with tears for those he warned (Luke 19:41).

Justice for the wronged

God’s justice is good news for victims. Those who have suffered great wrongs need not take revenge, because God will repay (Romans 12:19). No crime is finally lost or forgotten. Every wrong will either be paid for at the cross or answered at the judgment.

A woman wronged years ago by a business partner who was never held to account had carried a quiet rage ever since. Learning that God is just did two things for her. It assured her that the wrong mattered and would be answered. And it freed her from the job of making sure it was. She could leave it with the Judge of all the earth.

For reflection

Why would a God without wrath against evil be less loving, not more? How does Romans 3:25–26 answer the tension in Exodus 34:6–7? Is there a wrong done to you that you need to leave with God? Do you find it easier to believe in his justice for others, or his mercy for yourself?

5.title: Love, Goodness, Mercy and Patience
5.essay:
“God is love” (1 John 4:8). It is one of the shortest and most profound sentences in the Bible. It does not mean that love is God, so that whatever we feel as love is divine. It means that love is not something God does occasionally, but something he is.

God is love

Before creation, the Father loved the Son (John 17:24). Love is the life of the Trinity, and God’s love for us overflows from it. John tells us where to look to see it: “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 4:10). God’s love is not a feeling we must detect in our hearts; it is a fact accomplished in history. When we doubt it, we do not look inward. We look at the cross. And it is love for the unloving. We do not earn it by loving him; “we love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).

Scripture speaks of God’s love in more than one way. He loves all that he has made and is good to all (Psalm 145:9). He loves the world enough to send his Son and to call all people everywhere to repent (John 3:16; Acts 17:30). And he has a particular, saving love for his people — the love with which “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). Denying the first makes God cold toward the lost; denying the last makes his love vague and powerless.

God is good

“The LORD is good to all, and his mercy is over all that he has made” (Psalm 145:9). Every meal, sunrise, friendship and breath is a gift of his goodness, given to believers and unbelievers alike: he “makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good” (Matthew 5:45). Theologians call this common grace: rain, harvest, health, beauty, family and the restraint of evil, given to the whole world. Every unbeliever lives every day on the kindness of the God he ignores.

God is merciful

Mercy is God’s goodness toward those who are suffering or who deserve punishment. Psalm 103 explains it with pictures. “He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities. For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his steadfast love toward those who fear him; as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us. As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him. For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:10–14). God is not surprised by our weakness. He made us, and he deals with us gently.

Jesus told of a younger son who wasted his inheritance and came home rehearsing a speech about being made a servant. “But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (Luke 15:20). That is what God is like toward repentant sinners.

God is patient

God is “slow to anger”. He bears with sinners for years, giving them time to repent. When scoffers asked why Christ had not returned, Peter answered that God’s timing is not slowness but patience: “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). Every day the world goes on is a day of God’s patience, and God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11).

But patience has a purpose: God’s kindness “is meant to lead you to repentance” (Romans 2:4). To treat it as permission to keep sinning is to despise it. The day of patience will end.

Love and wrath together

These attributes are not soft spots in an otherwise stern God. They are what he chose to proclaim first when he revealed his glory (Exodus 34:6). God’s love does not cancel his wrath; it provides the answer to it. Love that never opposed evil would be indifference; wrath without love would leave us without hope. At the cross, God’s love bore God’s wrath. (Grace — God’s free favour to the undeserving — belongs here too, and has a study of its own.)

Living by his love

A Christian man had prayed for an unbelieving brother for thirty years and was tempted to give up. Reading 2 Peter 3:9, he realised God had been more patient with his brother than he had — and had been patient with him too, through years of his own wandering. He kept praying.

A simple test: when you sin, do you run from God or to him? Your answer shows what you really believe about his mercy.

For reflection

Where do you look when you doubt God’s love? Read Psalm 103 slowly: which picture of his mercy means most to you? Name three gifts of God’s goodness you received today. Who are you tempted to give up on, and how does God’s patience with you change that?

6.title: Faithful and True
6.essay:
Jerusalem had fallen. The temple was burned, the people were starving and the survivors were led away in chains. In the middle of the bleakest book in the Bible, the poet writes, “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:22–23). He did not say it because things were going well. He said it because God is faithful even when everything else has collapsed.

New every morning

These verses are the turning point of Lamentations. The poet has described his suffering in raw detail: God “has made my teeth grind on gravel” (Lamentations 3:16). Then he calls something to mind and has hope. God’s mercies are new every morning, like manna — enough for each day and no more. Faithfulness is not usually proved in one dramatic rescue. It is proved in daily provision through long sorrow.

God is true

God cannot lie (Titus 1:2; Hebrews 6:18). Everything he says is reliable. Jesus prayed, “your word is truth” (John 17:17). That is why Scripture can be trusted completely: it is the word of a God who does not deceive.

God is faithful

He keeps every promise, and his faithfulness does not depend on ours: “if we are faithless, he remains faithful — for he cannot deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13). This comes from a short early Christian saying whose earlier lines carry warnings (“if we deny him, he also will deny us”). But the last line turns on God’s own character. Even when his people are weak and failing, he remains faithful. He would have to stop being God to break his word.

“God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son” (1 Corinthians 1:9), and he will sustain his people to the end (1 Corinthians 1:8). When God wanted to give the strongest possible assurance, he added an oath to his promise — not because his word needed it, but for our sake — “so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us” (Hebrews 6:18). Notice who receives it: those who have fled for refuge. Assurance is for those who have run to Christ, not for those who trust in themselves.

The believer’s security rests not on the strength of his grip on God, but on God’s grip on him. Because God is faithful, those he justifies he also glorifies (Romans 8:30). True believers persevere not because they are strong, but because he does not let go.

Abraham waited twenty-five years for the promised son, and the promise seemed impossible. Yet he “grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God, fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised” (Romans 4:20–21). Faith is simply taking God at his word because of who he is.

The attributes become our life

God does not reveal himself only so that we can admire him from a distance. He means us to trust him, worship him and become like him. We cannot share his eternity or his presence everywhere. But by his Spirit we are being changed into the image of Christ (2 Corinthians 3:18), learning to be true, faithful, patient, merciful, just and loving in our small measure. “Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children. And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us” (Ephesians 5:1–2). God’s attributes are most fully seen in the cross, and most fully imitated in self-giving love.

The attributes God shares with us look very like the fruit of the Spirit: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Growth in holiness is growth in likeness to God. And every attribute is a reason for praise. The psalms rarely praise God in general; they praise him for something specific — his steadfast love, his faithfulness, his power, his works. Learning the attributes gives our worship words.

We shall see him

“We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). The study of God’s attributes is preparation for that day, and all eternity will not exhaust them.

A widow keeps a notebook. Each morning she writes down one thing about God from her Bible reading and one way she has seen it that day. After a year she has a record of God’s faithfulness in her grief, written in her own hand. Lamentations 3:23 is on the first page.

For reflection

Read Lamentations 3:1–33: how does the poet move from despair to hope? Which of God’s promises do you find hardest to believe right now? Which of his shared attributes do you most want to grow in? Choose one attribute from this study and use it to shape your praise this week.
